body:
A rival way to pose this: the question is not 'how do we make our agreements stick' but 'why does this household require so much agreement at all?' The input account treats vague agreements, schedule churn, mismatched standards, and conversation-avoidance as four separate faults to engineer around. The rival reading is that they are one fault with four faces: the shared domain is larger than the relationship's coordination capacity. On this reading the avoiding friend is not an obstacle to the fix but a measurement of the problem — they have already priced the conversations and found them more expensive than what they buy.

The levers change accordingly. First, shrink the commons instead of administering it better: privatize everything that can be privatized (own dishes, own laundry, own bathroom supplies), so that the list of genuinely shared chores becomes short. Second, prefer standing permanent ownership over rotas and swap rules — every swap rule is a standing invitation to renegotiate, and renegotiation is exactly what is failing. Rotas are the wrong shape not just because schedules change but because they maximize the number of agreements the household must hold simultaneously. Third, consider buying out: a cleaner every two weeks, cost split three ways, converts an endlessly re-litigated fairness question into a fixed bill, and is probably the largest available reduction in coordination load. It rarely gets proposed because it feels like defeat.

Fourth — and this is where the rival diverges most sharply from the input account — the asker's role. 'What should I do?' quietly installs the asker as household manager, a post nobody granted them. The input account's remedy (written note, definition of done, weekly check-in) is a management package, and arriving with one is itself a move in the conflict: it can read as 'I do not trust you,' which the account itself half-concedes by flagging that tracking may inflame. The rival's first move is smaller: ask each flatmate, separately, whether they think there is a problem worth a system at all, and what they would change. Their answers decide whether the next step is a system, a smaller commons, a cleaner, or nothing. For the avoider specifically, the offer is not a cheaper conversation but a smaller agenda: 'what would it take for this to stop being a recurring talk?'

Note that this does not discard the standards thread from the input account. Whatever survives shrinking still needs a minimum-standards conversation; the rival only reduces that conversation's blast radius. And there is a checkable prediction to separate the two framings: if overload is right, reducing the count of agreements should reduce both the re-arguing and the avoidance even with no change in anyone's fairness perceptions. If disputes persist at the same rate per agreement, overload was wrong and the problem is genuinely about trust or standards.
commitments:
The load-bearing claims here are conjectures, and taking this up means treating them as such. The claim that avoidance signals coordination overload rather than conflict-aversion or disengagement is testable in principle — by counting how many distinct agreements the household is maintaining, shrinking that count, and watching whether avoidance and re-litigation fall — but the test is confounded, since any shrink also changes what people argue about, and a drop in disputes could reflect fewer occasions rather than less friction. The claim that rotas and swap rules generate renegotiation load beyond what schedule churn explains is reasoning, not observation; nothing in the exposed material shows whether these flatmates actually renegotiate often or simply fail to comply.

The cleaner proposal carries explicit dependences: money from all three, willingness to spend it on this, and enough residual goodwill to organize the hire — which is itself a conversation, the scarce resource. If that conversation cannot be had, the buyout is moot. The 'ask before proposing' step depends on the avoider answering even a low-stakes question; silence there does not distinguish overload from withdrawal from the friendship, and the two call for different responses.

A live criticism of the whole framing: privatization is easy for dishes and impossible for the hallway floor, so some irreducible commons remains, and shrinking may simply concentrate resentment on the lowest-threshold flatmate, who ends up owning the residual by default. A second criticism: reducing the shared surface could confirm distance rather than relieve it, if any of the three experiences joint chores as part of what makes this a friendship rather than a tenancy arrangement. Both criticisms stand against the rival as posed and are not answered here.

Unresolved: if both flatmates answer 'no problem worth a system' while chores still go undone, the asker faces a choice the framing does not resolve — accept the resulting household standard, or treat flat-shares as compatibilities that can expire and consider moving. As a proposed application, the ordering is: individual asks first, scope reduction second, cleaner quote third, and only for the small surviving list would the input account's definition-of-done discipline be adopted — administration last and minimal rather than first and maximal. That sequencing is itself a claim about what inflames versus reassures, open to revision if the first one-on-ones go badly.
